strengths: First systematic attempt to apply hypergraph modeling and explicit high-order interaction (HOI) reasoning to audio deepfake detection (ADD), a domain that has predominantly relied on pairwise/local relational modules (attention, graph edges, convolutions).

The overall architecture is well-engineered: FCM-based soft hyperedge construction, a relational artifact amplification operator combining structural and feature-level self-similarity, and a class-aware prototype bank with EMA updates and a two-stage (soft/slot) alignment scheme for cross-batch consistency are all clearly described with equations.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 13 diverse test sets (different languages, codecs, spoofing methods, and 'in-the-wild' conditions), with consistent training-only-on-ASVspoof2019LA protocol, following the Speech DF Arena benchmark, which supports a reasonably standardized generalization study.

Multiple complementary analyses beyond aggregate EER/F1 numbers: hyperedge-cardinality distribution histograms, dataset-level clustermaps of relational similarity, PCA of prototype banks/aligned centroids, and sample-level segment analysis on PartialSpoof, which together provide some qualitative evidence that the learned hyperedges capture non-trivial multi-node relations rather than degenerating to pairwise edges.

Reasonably thorough ablations on sub-modules (amplification module, prototype banks, alignment algorithms) and on hyperedge count/degree hyperparameters, plus an additional ablation replacing AASIST's heterogeneous attention layer with the proposed HAGNN in a non-SSL setting, showing the idea is not entirely tied to one backbone.

Negative/mixed results (e.g., degradation on 2021LA and ASVspoof5, codec augmentation trade-offs) are reported rather than hidden, and the paper attempts to explain them via a channel-distortion hypothesis, which is a positive sign of honest reporting.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation (Section 3, O-information/synergy-dominated hypothesis) is never actually quantified on real ADD features: the paper introduces the C(Xn), B(Xn), Ω(Xn) formalism in detail but does not compute these quantities for actual embeddings from ASVspoof/other datasets to verify that ADD systems are indeed synergy-dominated (Ω<0). The claimed empirical support in Figure 1 (right) is instead just aggregated performance gains in Table 6, which is not evidence about the sign or magnitude of O-information; this leaves the theoretical framing largely rhetorical/post-hoc rather than empirically validated, undermining the 'first investigation of high-order effects...from an information-theoretic perspective' claim.

Inconsistent headline numbers: the abstract reports a 22.15% average relative gain across 11 datasets, while the conclusion states a 15.32% average relative gain across 13 datasets; this discrepancy is not explained and raises concerns about result reporting consistency/rigor.

Performance is inconsistent across benchmarks: HyperPotter underperforms its own baseline on ASVspoof2021LA and ASVspoof5 (Table 1), and the 'Strong Distortion' scenario in Table 6 also shows a decrease relative to baseline; the explanation ('channel interference masks HOIs') is speculative and not directly tested (e.g., no controlled experiment isolating distortion severity vs. Ω sign).

Several SOTA baselines in Table 1/5 have missing entries ('-') for many datasets, so the comparison to prior state-of-the-art is incomplete for many rows, making it hard to assess whether HyperPotter is truly SOTA across the full benchmark suite rather than only against its own retrained baseline.

No variance/statistical significance reporting: all results appear to be single-run numbers (no seeds, standard deviations, or significance tests), which is a concern given some of the EER differences (e.g., third-best vs baseline) are small and the method has many hyperparameters (β1, β2, τ, m, K, D, μ, γ, warm-start schedule) that could be tuned per-dataset.

The technical novelty is largely a recombination of existing techniques (Fuzzy C-Means clustering, hypergraph attention, EMA-based prototype memory, attention amplification) applied to a new domain, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution; the paper would benefit from more explicit justification of why this particular combination is necessary versus simpler high-order alternatives.

No analysis of computational overhead (training/inference time, FCM iteration cost) despite the added architectural complexity (multiple HAGNN layers, iterative FCM clustering, prototype bank maintenance), which matters for practical deployment claims.

The interpretive narrative in Sec 6.2 (positioning HyperPotter as a 'specialist' suited for MoE ensembles when it underperforms under channel distortion) reads as a post-hoc rationalization of weaknesses rather than a rigorously tested claim, and is not supported by any ensemble or MoE experiments in the paper.

strengths: Novel framing of audio deepfake detection through the lens of high-order interactions (HOIs) and O-information theory, providing a fresh conceptual angle relative to the dominant pairwise/graph-attention paradigm in ADD.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 13 cross-scenario test sets, comparisons with numerous recent SOTA methods, thorough ablations (sub-modules, alignment algorithms, hyperedge count/cardinality, FCM iterations), stability across seeds, scalability to longer audio, and detailed computational cost analysis (latency/throughput/VRAM) in the appendix.

Honest and detailed limitations discussion: the paper explicitly identifies and analyzes degradation under codec/channel distortion (21LA, ASVspoof5), rather than hiding negative results, and explores augmentation remedies.

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode for the hypergraph attention layer, dataset descriptions, and development-set robustness checks (Appendix B.2) that test sensitivity of checkpoint selection to different dev sets.

Interesting diagnostic visualizations (O-information heatmaps, hyperedge cardinality distributions, PCA of prototype banks, sample-level segment analysis) that offer some qualitative support for the high-order relational modeling claim.
weaknesses: The connection between the O-information theoretical motivation (Section 3) and the actual method (Sections 4-5) is loose: the FCM/hypergraph/prototype architecture is not derived from or optimized to explicitly increase synergy or O-information; the O-information analysis is a post-hoc diagnostic overlay rather than an integral part of the training objective, and the authors themselves concede they are not offering "a formal decomposition into pure redundancy or pure synergy," weakening the causal story linking theory to design choices.

Performance gains are inconsistent: the method underperforms the baseline on 2 of 13 sets (21LA, ASVspoof5) and ablations show that removing key modules (amplification, prototypes) sometimes *improves* results on these same codec-heavy sets, suggesting the architecture is not clearly principled but rather empirically tuned to the majority of test conditions, undermining the generality of the core "HOI is important" claim.

Non-trivial computational overhead: Table 13 shows roughly 3-4x higher per-sample latency and substantially lower throughput than the baseline across batch sizes, which is a significant practical cost for a method whose average relative EER reduction (12.68%) is meaningful but not transformative, especially given failure cases under distortion that are common in real deployment (telephony/codec channels).

Many architectural hyperparameters (β1, β2, warm-start epoch schedule, similarity gate decay, slot/soft alignment epoch boundaries) appear to be manually fixed based on "early model design" without systematic justification, raising concerns about overfitting to the specific benchmark suite and limiting confidence in generalizability to new settings.

The novelty is primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques (FCM soft clustering, hypergraph attention, prototype-guided initialization borrowed from domain adaptation/incremental learning) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical contribution; the claimed "first investigation of HOI in ADD via O-information" is more of a novel analytical framing than a rigorously validated new mechanism.

Some result tables have missing baseline entries (dashes) making several cross-method comparisons incomplete, and reported baseline numbers sometimes diverge from other published results, which could reflect reproduction variance not fully discussed in the main text.

strengths: Novel problem framing: the paper is the first to systematically motivate audio deepfake detection (ADD) via high-order interactions (HOIs) and to ground this motivation with a principled information-theoretic tool (O-information), providing an interesting conceptual bridge between redundancy/synergy theory and hypergraph-based ADD modeling.

The proposed HyperPotter architecture is reasonably well engineered, combining FCM-based soft hyperedge construction, an attention-driven relational artifact amplification module, and a class-aware prototype bank with EMA updates and soft/slot alignment for cross-batch consistency.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 13 cross-scenario test sets covering different languages, codecs, and spoofing methods, plus substantial appendix material (F1 scores, additional datasets such as EmoFake/MLAAD/SingFake, scalability to 8s audio, stability across three random seeds, sensitivity to hyperparameters K/R/T, and detailed complexity/latency/VRAM analysis).

Honest and detailed limitations discussion: the paper explicitly identifies and analyzes degraded performance under severe codec/channel distortion (21LA, ASVspoof5) rather than hiding it, and offers a plausible explanation (distortion masking fine-grained relational structure).

Good ablation coverage isolating the amplification module, prototype banks, and the two alignment algorithms, as well as hyperedge count/cardinality sweeps, which helps substantiate (to some extent) the necessity of HOI modeling over pure pairwise mechanisms.

Rich qualitative and quantitative interpretability analysis (O-information heatmaps, hyperedge cardinality distributions, dataset/sample-level clustering, PCA of prototype banks) that gives some insight into what the hypergraph module is learning.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim (that ADD artifacts are predominantly synergy-dominated and hypergraphs capture this better than pairwise graphs) is only supported by suggestive, qualitative O-information visualizations (Fig. 3) on learned centroids; the authors themselves concede this is not a rigorous decomposition, weakening the causal link between the theoretical motivation and the proposed architecture.

Gains are inconsistent across several important, non-trivial evaluation sets (2021LA, ASVspoof5, and some ADD tracks show performance degradation relative to baseline), and the ablations show that removing the amplification module or prototype banks actually improves results on 21LA/ASVspoof5 in some configurations — this undercuts the generality of the core claim that HOI modeling is broadly beneficial.

Substantial added computational cost: Table 13 shows roughly 3-4x higher per-batch inference/training latency and markedly lower throughput than the baseline for only a modest average EER improvement, which limits the practical significance of the method, especially since the paper does not compare this added cost against other competitive SOTA baselines.

The checkpoint/model-selection protocol uses a held-out subset of the In-the-Wild (ITW) dataset for early stopping, while ITW itself is one of the headline test sets reported in the main comparison table; although the paper attempts to address this with alternative dev-set reruns (Appendix B.2), the practice of tuning against a dataset that doubles as a primary reported benchmark raises fairness/leakage concerns relative to baselines that do not use such tailored selection.

The framework has many heuristically chosen design elements (similarity gate schedule, 20%/80% prototype slot allocation, specific epoch thresholds for switching alignment strategies, fusion weights β1/β2) whose individual necessity is not fully justified via ablation, raising concerns about overfitting to the specific benchmark suite and about reproducibility of these choices in new settings.

Baseline SOTA comparisons in Table 1 mix self-reproduced results with numbers copied from original papers under potentially different training/evaluation protocols, which can introduce inconsistencies that are hard for readers to control for when judging the significance of the reported improvements.
